mcq.q: Which query is BM25 likely to handle better than dense retrieval?
options: "my card keeps getting declined"
"error E-4012"
"how do I feel valued at work"
"summarise our culture"
mcq.why: Exact identifiers and codes favour lexical matching.
distractors: Paraphrased complaints are where dense retrieval's meaning-matching helps.
A vague, emotional query suits dense retrieval better.
There are no exact terms to match; dense retrieval does better here.

mcq.q: What is an inverted index?
options: A reversed copy of each document, read from the end
A list of all documents, sorted by their length
A vector store holding one embedding per document
A map from each term to the documents containing it
mcq.why: Finding “refund” means reading one posting list.
distractors: Nothing is reversed; terms point to documents.
Sorting by length does not find terms.

mcq.q: How do TF-IDF and BM25 score a document?
options: By query-term frequency, weighted by how rare each term is
By embedding similarity between the query and each document
By document length, so shorter documents rank higher
By the document's date, so newer documents rank higher
mcq.why: Rare terms carry more weight than common ones.
distractors: Length is only a normalisation factor.
Dates are metadata, not BM25 scoring.

mcq.q: What does BM25's saturation parameter k₁ do?
options: Penalises long documents for their length
Makes each extra occurrence add less
Controls the size of the embedding vectors
Sets the number of results that are returned
mcq.why: The tenth occurrence adds little.

mcq.q: What does BM25's parameter b do?
options: Controls how quickly repeated terms saturate
Sets the vocabulary size of the inverted index
Normalises for length, so long documents are not favoured
Boosts recent documents in the ranking
mcq.why: Typically b ≈ 0.75.
distractors: Recency is not part of BM25.

mcq.q: With N = 8 documents and a term in 1 of them, what is IDF = ln(1 + (N − n + 0.5)/(n + 0.5))?
options: About 1.79
About 0.69
About 2.08

mcq.q: BM25 finds nothing for “can't log in” because the documents say “login” and “sign in”. What is this called, and what helps?
options: Overfitting; more training data helps
Vocabulary mismatch; dense retrieval helps
Latency; caching the results helps
Contamination; deduplication helps
mcq.why: Dense retrieval matches meaning across different words.
distractors: The failure is about matching words.

mcq.q: What is learned sparse retrieval (for example SPLADE)?
options: BM25 run without the IDF weighting, to make indexing faster
A model weights vocabulary terms, related ones too, in an inverted index
Dense vectors stored on disk instead of in memory, to save RAM
A cross-encoder reranker run over the keyword search results
mcq.why: It combines keyword-index efficiency with some semantic matching.
distractors: It is a learned model, not a BM25 variant.
SPLADE weights vocabulary terms; it is sparse.
Rerankers re-score; SPLADE builds the index.

mcq.q: A team assumes their vector database chose a good embedding model. What is wrong?
options: Embedding models are all the same, so any choice works
Vector databases train the embedding model on your data
Nothing; the database vendor tests models for each corpus
A vector DB only stores and searches; the model is your choice
mcq.why: Evaluate embedding models on your queries.
distractors: Models differ greatly by domain and language.
They store and search vectors only.
Only your own evaluation shows fit.

mcq.q: Why does BM25 need no training?
options: It uses an LLM to score terms
It uses corpus term statistics
It is pretrained by its vendor
It learns weights from clicks
mcq.why: Counts and document frequencies are all it needs.
distractors: It is a formula, not a model.
Click learning is learning to rank.

mcq.q: In a 10,000-document corpus, “refund” appears in 9,000 documents and “E-4012” in 3. Using BM25's IDF = ln(1 + (N − n + 0.5)/(n + 0.5)), which term weighs more, and roughly by how much?
options: “E-4012”: IDF about 7.9 against about 0.1 for “refund”
“E-4012”: about 3 against 9,000, by raw document counts
“refund”: it appears far more often, so it weighs more
They weigh the same, since IDF ignores how common terms are
distractors: IDF uses the log of an inverse ratio, not raw counts.
IDF rewards rarity; common terms weigh little.
IDF is exactly about how common a term is.

mcq.q: Why use reciprocal rank fusion?
options: It needs no normalisation of different score scales
It is the most accurate reranker for the top results
It replaces the embedding model in dense retrieval
It reduces the size of both the vector and keyword indexes
mcq.why: RRF uses ranks only, so BM25 and cosine scores need not share a scale.
distractors: Accuracy comes from rerankers; RRF fuses lists.
RRF fuses rankings that still come from embeddings and keywords.
Fusion happens at query time and does not change the index.

mcq.q: Where must permission filtering happen?
options: In the prompt, by telling the model what not to use
After generation, by checking the answer for leaks
In retrieval, before content reaches the model
In the UI, by hiding results the user may not see
mcq.why: Once the model has seen restricted text, the leak has already happened.
distractors: A prompt instruction cannot stop leaked content from being read.
After generation the content has already reached the model.
Hiding content in the UI still leaves it in the model's answer.

mcq.q: With RRF (k = 60), a document ranked 1st by BM25 and 3rd by dense search scores what?
options: About 0.25
About 0.0164
About 0.0323
distractors: That counts only the BM25 rank.

mcq.q: What does a cross-encoder reranker do?
options: Embeds each document separately for fast search
Filters the results by the user's permissions
Reads query and passage together; re-scores the top 50–200
Generates the final answer from the passages
mcq.why: Much more accurate than separate embeddings, but too slow for the whole corpus.
distractors: Filters run before or during retrieval.

mcq.q: What is the difference between pre-filtering and post-filtering?
options: Post-filtering is always faster, since search runs once
They are the same, just applied by different services
Pre-filtering is done by the user in the search box
Pre-filtering filters during search; post-filtering removes results after
mcq.why: Selective post-filters can leave too few results.
distractors: Speed depends; selectivity is the key issue.
When the filter runs changes the results.

mcq.q: A highly selective filter is applied after retrieving the top 20. What can happen?
options: Results improve in relevance
Too few results remain
Nothing happens to the results
The index grows to compensate
mcq.why: Apply selective filters inside the search.
distractors: Removing results does not improve the rest.
A selective filter removes most of them.
Filters do not change the index.

mcq.q: Which steps belong to context assembly?
options: Embed the query and search the index
Train the reranker on click data
Choose the GPU for serving the model
Dedupe, merge, order, label, fit the budget
mcq.why: Assembly prepares what the model sees (7.3).

mcq.q: A team adds raw BM25 scores to cosine similarities to rank results. What is wrong?
options: Cosine scores are always larger, so they dominate
Different scales: fuse by rank (RRF) or normalise carefully
Nothing, as long as both scores are positive
BM25 scores are probabilities, so they can be added
mcq.why: RRF needs no score normalisation because it uses ranks.
distractors: BM25 scores are usually larger; the issue is scale.

mcq.q: What is a typical latency budget for filters plus retrieval, and for reranking on GPU?
options: Retrieval about 5 s; reranking about 10 s
Both well under 1 ms on any hardware
Retrieval 30–80 ms; reranking 50–200 ms
Retrieval about 1 s; reranking about 1 hour
mcq.why: Reranking is slower on CPU.
distractors: Far too slow for interactive use.
Reranking a list takes tens of milliseconds.

mcq.q: In RRF, what does a small k do?
options: Emphasises the top ranks more
Flattens the differences between ranks
Changes which retrievers are used
Removes documents from the fused list
mcq.why: Large k flattens differences.

mcq.q: With RRF and k = 60, document X is ranked 1st by BM25 and 30th by dense search; Y is 5th by both. Which ranks higher after fusion?
options: X: about 0.0328 against about 0.0154 for Y
Y: about 0.0308 against about 0.0275 for X
X, because a first place always wins in fusion
They tie, because their average ranks are equal
mcq.why: X: 1/61 + 1/90 ≈ 0.0275. Y: 2 × 1/65 ≈ 0.0308. Being found well by both lists beats one first place.
distractors: That counts X's first place twice and Y's fifth place once.
RRF sums contributions; a weak second rank pulls X down.
RRF sums reciprocal ranks, not average ranks.

mcq.q: What kind of problem does RAG solve, and what kind does fine-tuning solve?
options: RAG: a knowledge problem; fine-tuning: a behaviour problem
RAG: a behaviour problem; fine-tuning: a knowledge problem
Both solve latency
Neither changes outputs
mcq.why: RAG supplies missing facts with sources; fine-tuning changes format, style or decision patterns.

mcq.q: Why is fine-tuning a poor way to inject facts?
options: It is too cheap, so teams overuse it and skip retrieval
It always makes the model forget the required output format
Costly to update, hard to delete, no citations, unreliable recall
It needs no data, so the facts it adds may well be wrong
mcq.why: Facts belong in retrievable, citable, deletable sources.
distractors: It is relatively expensive to repeat.
Format is what fine-tuning teaches well.
It needs data, and that is not the problem.

mcq.q: Policies change every week and answers must cite them. Which approach fits?
options: A longer system prompt
RAG
Continued pretraining
Fine-tuning weekly
mcq.why: Re-index on change and cite policy IDs.
distractors: Does not scale to thousands of policies.

mcq.q: Answers are correct but not in the mandated format, and few-shot prompting costs too many tokens. What fits?
options: A small format fine-tune, keeping RAG
A bigger model, with the same prompt
Removing RAG and relying on the model
Continued pretraining on the formats
mcq.why: A behaviour gap that prompting cannot close cheaply.
distractors: Size does not enforce a format.
That is for domain language, not a format.

mcq.q: What should you always start with?
options: An agent framework with tool calls
Pretraining a model on company data
Prompting plus RAG; fine-tune for measured gaps
Fine-tuning on past conversations
mcq.why: Fine-tune when evidence says prompting cannot close the gap (13.1).
distractors: Agents add complexity before it is needed.
Far too costly as a start.
Fine-tune only for a measured gap.

mcq.q: A fact was fine-tuned into a model, and the source document has now been deleted. What happens to the fact?
options: The model asks for the document
It may remain in the weights
It disappears automatically
The model refuses to mention it
mcq.why: Deleting the source does not remove what the weights learned.

mcq.q: Users need answers traceable to sources. Which approach provides that?
options: Fine-tuning
RAG with citations
A bigger vocabulary
Higher temperature
mcq.why: Retrieved chunks carry IDs to cite.

mcq.q: The model lacks long-tail facts about your niche products. What helps most?
options: Removing the system prompt to free tokens
Shorter answers with fewer claims
Retrieving those facts at question time
Raising the temperature for variety
mcq.why: Long-tail facts are a knowledge gap.
distractors: Shorter answers do not supply facts.

mcq.q: Which statement describes using both approaches together?
options: RAG supplies facts; a fine-tune shapes format
Fine-tuning supplies facts; RAG supplies the format
They cannot be combined in one system
Using both removes the need for evaluation
mcq.why: The bank example in the topic does exactly this.

mcq.q: Why might a team fine-tune for format instead of using few-shot examples?
options: Fine-tuning is always cheaper than prompting
Prompts cannot be versioned or reviewed
Few-shot examples cost tokens on every call
Few-shot examples cannot show a format
mcq.why: Repeated examples add cost and latency to every request.
distractors: They can; they are just costly.

interview.q: When would you use RAG, fine-tuning, or both?
covers: Both when facts and format both matter

covers: Format via prompt or small fine-tune

interview.q: How do you handle a user's request to delete their data when a model may have been trained on it?
covers: Prefer retrieval so data can be deleted at the source
Track what data went into each fine-tune
Retrain or retire models if needed
interview.followUp: How would you track which data went into each fine-tune?

mcq.q: Which RAG stages run offline, and which online?
options: Ingest to index offline; retrieve and generate per question
All stages run online, once for every new question
All stages run offline, before any question is asked
Only generation runs offline, in nightly batches of answers
mcq.why: Offline stages run continuously at scale (chapter 10).
distractors: Parsing and embedding a corpus per question is far too slow.

mcq.q: Which stage caps the quality of everything downstream?
options: Parsing
Rendering citations
Generation
Logging
mcq.why: Text lost or garbled in parsing cannot be retrieved later (10.3).
distractors: Generation depends on what retrieval provides.

mcq.q: What is a typical chunk size, and how should chunks be split?
options: Exactly 4,096 characters each, cut wherever the limit falls
A whole document each, however long the document is
One sentence each, with no headings or other context
~200–800 tokens, on headings and paragraphs, small overlaps
mcq.why: Small enough to be specific, large enough to be self-contained.
distractors: Fixed cuts break sentences and rules.

mcq.q: Why prepend a header such as the document title and section path to each chunk?
options: To speed up the model at query time
To hide the chunk's content from search
So each chunk makes sense on its own
To make every chunk the same length
mcq.why: “The limit is 5 days per year” becomes unambiguous with its section path.
distractors: Headers add context; they hide nothing.

mcq.q: What does chunk overlap do?
options: Reduces the storage the index needs
Removes duplicate chunks from the index
Speeds up retrieval at query time
Keeps boundary sentences whole, costing storage
mcq.why: Overlapping text appears in two chunks.
distractors: It does not affect speed much.

mcq.q: Why record the embedding model's name and version with each vector?
options: For decoration in the admin interface
A new model means re-embedding everything
To speed up search across the index
Because vectors are stored as text
mcq.why: Vectors from different models are not comparable.

mcq.q: What does the index store?
options: Vectors (ANN), text (keyword) and metadata
Only the original PDFs, for re-parsing
Only the vectors, for semantic search
Only the metadata, for filtering
mcq.why: Hybrid search and permission filters need all three.
distractors: Keyword search and filters need more.
Text and vectors are needed too.

mcq.q: Fixed-size chunks cut a rule away from its exception. What fixes it?
options: A bigger, stronger model to write the answers
Removing the overlap between neighbouring chunks
Structure-aware chunking that keeps sections whole
Smaller chunks of a fixed size, with more of them
mcq.why: The chunking figure shows this directly.
distractors: The model never sees both together.

mcq.q: PDF parsing is poor and answers are wrong. A team switches to a stronger answer model. What is likely?
options: Retrieval improves automatically
Costs fall with the stronger model
Little gain: fix parsing first
Answers become correct at last
mcq.why: The model cannot use text that parsing lost.
distractors: The parsed text is still broken.

mcq.q: 10,000 documents average 3,000 tokens each. With 500-token chunks and no overlap, about how many chunks is that?
mcq.why: 6 chunks per document × 10,000 documents.

mcq.q: A refund policy chunk reads “Refunds are allowed within 30 days” with no title or section. A query about “electronics returns” misses it, though the section was about electronics. What fix does the topic suggest?
options: Raise top-k until the chunk appears somewhere in the results
Remove the overlap between chunks to keep them distinct
Use smaller chunks so each one holds a single short sentence
Prepend the document title and section path to each chunk before embedding
mcq.why: The header gives the chunk context it lacks, so it can be retrieved and cited on its own.
distractors: That adds noise without fixing the chunk.
Overlap is not why the context is missing.
Smaller chunks lose even more context.

mcq.q: Brute-force search over 10 million 768-dimension vectors takes about how many multiply-adds per query?
options: About 768
About 7.7 billion
About 7.7 million
About 10 million
distractors: Three orders of magnitude too low.

mcq.q: What do approximate nearest-neighbour (ANN) indexes trade?
options: Nothing; results are identical
Speed in exchange for exactness
Accuracy for smaller storage only
A little recall for much more speed
mcq.why: Exact search is fine for thousands of vectors, too slow for millions at high query rates.
distractors: It is the other way round.

mcq.q: How does HNSW search work?
options: Compare the query with every vector in turn
Hash the vectors into buckets and scan one
Start at a sparse top layer and descend greedily
Cluster the vectors and search one cluster
mcq.why: Upper layers act as express lanes with long links.

mcq.q: Which HNSW parameter controls the recall–latency trade-off at query time?
options: efSearch
M
efConstruction
nprobe
mcq.why: More candidates explored means higher recall and more latency.
distractors: M sets links per node (memory and recall).

mcq.q: How does an IVF index search?
options: Walk a layered graph from a sparse top layer downwards
Cluster with k-means; search the nearest nprobe clusters
Use an inverted index from terms to documents
Scan every vector in the index and keep the closest
mcq.why: More probes raise recall and cost.

mcq.q: How much memory do 10 million 768-dimension float32 vectors need?
options: About 7.7 GB
About 3.1 GB
About 30.7 GB
About 307 GB
mcq.why: 10⁷ × 768 × 4 bytes ≈ 30.7 GB, before index overhead.

mcq.q: With int8 scalar quantisation instead of float32, how large are those vectors?
options: About 15.4 GB
About 0.96 GB
About 7.7 GB
About 30.7 GB
mcq.why: 4× smaller than float32. Binary would be about 0.96 GB (32× smaller).

mcq.q: What is the common pattern for searching quantised vectors?
options: Never use the full-precision vectors again
Search compressed vectors, re-score with full ones
Delete the original vectors to save space
Quantise only the query, not the stored vectors
mcq.why: Re-scoring recovers most of the lost recall.
distractors: Full precision is used to re-score.
The stored vectors are what shrink.

mcq.q: efSearch 40 gives Recall@10 0.91 at 2 ms; efSearch 200 gives 0.985 at 7 ms. How should you choose?
options: Randomly, since the difference is small
Always the highest recall available
Always the fastest setting available
By the cost of a miss versus the latency budget
mcq.why: The right point depends on the application.
distractors: The gap matters for some uses.
A missed chunk can be costly.

mcq.q: Retrieved passages are the wrong ones, though ANN recall against exact search is 0.99. What will raising ANN recall do?
options: Little: the embeddings rank the wrong passages close
Fix it completely, since higher recall finds better passages
Make it worse, because a slower search returns fewer results
Change the passages' text so they match the query better
mcq.why: ANN recall measures agreement with exact search, not relevance.
distractors: ANN recall measures agreement with exact search.
It would barely change the passages.
ANN settings do not change text.

covers: Brute force cost grows with corpus size
ANN trades a little recall for speed
Fine to use exact search for small corpora

mcq.q: What does query rewriting do?
options: Turns follow-ups into standalone search queries
Translates the documents into the user's language
Removes citations from the generated answer
Compresses the answer to fit the window
mcq.why: “What about for contractors?” needs the earlier context.
distractors: It rewrites the query, not documents.

mcq.q: What is HyDE?
options: A cross-encoder reranker for the top results
A chunking method that splits long documents
A vector database built for hybrid search
Embedding a generated answer instead of the question
mcq.why: The hypothetical answer may sit closer to relevant passages in embedding space.

mcq.q: What is decomposition?
options: Splitting documents into single sentences
Lowering the numeric precision of vectors
Splitting a compound question into sub-queries
Deleting old chunks from the index
mcq.why: For example, comparing policies in two countries.

mcq.q: What is multi-hop retrieval?
options: A chain of searches, each using the last one's fact
Using two embedding models in parallel and fusing them
Retrieving the same query twice for redundancy
Searching a keyword and a vector index at once
mcq.why: It is an iterative loop, effectively a small agent.
distractors: That is an ensemble, not a chain.
Repeats do not use new facts.

mcq.q: What keeps multi-hop retrieval from searching endlessly?
options: More chunks retrieved per hop
A hop limit and an abstain path
A higher sampling temperature
A bigger, smarter planner model
mcq.why: For example, at most 3 hops, then abstain.
distractors: More chunks do not stop a loop.
Size does not bound the loop.

mcq.q: How should citations be verified?
options: Count them and require at least one per answer
Check they are formatted as clickable links
Trust the model, which chose the sources
In code: labels exist and the chunk supports the claim
mcq.why: Then render citations as links to the source.

mcq.q: Retrieval scores are low and nothing supports an answer. What should the assistant do?
options: Guess politely and add a disclaimer
Retry retrieval until something is found
Abstain and offer a next step
Answer confidently from general knowledge
mcq.why: A confident wrong answer is worse than an honest “not found”.
distractors: That risks a confident wrong answer.

mcq.q: A user asks “what about for contractors?” after a question about leave. What must happen before retrieval?
options: Rewrite it as a standalone query using history
Search the words exactly as typed
Refuse until the user rephrases it
Ask the model to guess the topic
mcq.why: The follow-up alone is ambiguous.
distractors: “What about for contractors?” retrieves nothing useful.

mcq.q: An answer cites a whole 80-page document. What is the problem?
options: Nothing, as long as the link works
It does not point to the clause relied on
The document is too short to be cited
Citations must point to dates, not documents
mcq.why: Cite the specific chunk.
distractors: The reader cannot find the supporting clause.
They must point to the supporting passage.

mcq.q: When should you add multi-hop retrieval?
options: When evaluation shows single-shot fails
Only for short, simple questions
Always, for every question asked
Never; single-shot retrieval is enough
mcq.why: Each hop adds latency and a chance of error.

mcq.q: “Compare parental leave in Germany and the UK” retrieves only German policy chunks. Which technique addresses this?
options: Raise the reranker's threshold so that fewer, better chunks pass
Decompose it into one sub-query per country, retrieve for each, then synthesise

A hop limit with an abstain path for whatever results are missing
mcq.why: A compound question needs a retrieval per part; one query favours whichever part matches best.
distractors: Fewer chunks make the gap worse.
One hypothetical answer may still lean towards one country.
Abstaining does not fetch the missing UK policy.
